name: Mummy (मम्मी), 52

voice.register: Brisk, mid-fast and level: the pace of a shop counter on a Saturday, warm underneath, never cold, never loud. MEDIUM length, the middle of the cast. She has two shapes, and the job of the line picks the shape. ORDERS, PLANS, A NO AND A SCHEDULE come as one comma list of people and jobs (or goods), five to ten words, closed by one full stop and usually with no verb: 'Tum bill, Tinku stock, main shutter.'. CARE AND COMFORT get their verb back: short whole sentences with hai or hoon in them ('Shutter hai, counter hai, haath hain.', 'Main glass laati hoon.', 'Sab bag mein hai.'), so she is not one more clipped voice in a house that already has five. A second thought is a second bubble, never a longer one. Her list is people and jobs; it is not Nani's closed one-to-three-word fragments, not Captain sahab's call and then a reason, not Mami's item-and-status readback, and not Papa's run of whole sentences. HUMOUR: none on purpose. She is the straight face; the family laughs at her shop voice at home ('Haan ji, boliye.' to her own children, 'Aur kuch?' at a goodbye) and she never hears the joke. FEELING is changed into shop news with no figure ('Copper phir mehenga.'); love is mostly a deed, and when it is spoken it is a packed list that keeps its hai. CROSS: very still, the voice drops, and politeness rises. The one slow subject is her roof chillies: there the list stops and she says whole, unhurried sentences.
voice.mix: A Hindi frame, the everyday Hindi of a small Hindi-speaking junction town, with English nouns from today's counter dropped in whole: shutter, stock, bill, counter, delivery, godown, customer, fuse, wire, switch, fan, bulb, copper, MCB, mains, extension. The English verb + kar/ho ('check karo', 'delivery ho gayi') is the commonest Hinglish pattern in India and the whole house shares it; what marks her is where she aims it. The shop's words come home with her, as they do in any electrician's house: a power cut at dinner is 'MCB check karo', the water at the door is 'mains off karo'. No whole English clauses (Mama ji and Mami switch clause by clause). The common Hindi fillers are hers as much as anyone's (achha, haan, haan ji, chalo, suno, dekho, bas, theek hai, arre inside a line), and so are the everyday Urdu-rooted town words (zaroor, waqt, zaroorat). What her English carries: goods. Hindi mode keeps the trade nouns in Devanagari as Hindi speakers say them (शटर, स्टॉक, बिल, चेक करो). Her credit book is 'khaata' | खाता in both scripts, as every small-town shop says it, and the word means only that book. English mode is Indian English as it is spoken, not a word-for-word copy: 'Haan ji, boliye.' is 'Yes, tell me.', 'Aur kuch?' is 'Anything else?', 'Had hai!' is 'This is too much!', and the rising 'ji' stays on names when she is cross (Tinku ji, Chhote ji). Her two marked figures are said in words in speech ('nau baje', 'nau bajkar das'), which collide with no other word (unlike 'saath'); in typing a figure is a digit.
tics: Answers every phone call with the shop greeting, 'Haan ji, boliye.' | 'हाँ जी, बोलिए।' | 'Yes, tell me.', to Nani and to you exactly as to a customer. When she knows the voice she drops to तुम with 'Achha, tum.' and carries on, so the reader hears the switch and never takes it for a slip. This is her first tell.

Orders, plans and a no come as one comma list of people and jobs, five to ten words, ticked off on the fingers of her left hand: 'Tum bill, Tinku stock, main shutter.'. Comfort keeps the list's bones but gets its verb: 'Shutter hai, counter hai, haath hain.'.

Closes a talk the way she closes a sale: 'Aur kuch?' | 'और कुछ?' | 'Anything else?', after a compliment, at a goodbye, when asked how she is. At most one bubble in four, because Mami's 'Correct?' holds the cast's other closing question.
Changes a feeling into shop news with no figure: 'How are you, Mummy?' 'Copper phir mehenga.' The dodge is hers alone; Papa and Tinku drop theirs (C10).

The shop's English comes home: the English verb + kar/ho that the whole house uses, carrying the trade words of an electrician's house: 'MCB check karo.', 'Mains off karo.'. Never a joke on the kitchen: a too-sweet tea is plain 'Cheeni kam, dobara banao.'.
When cross, politeness rises instead of volume: 'ji' goes onto names that never carry it ('Tinku ji', 'Chhote ji'), तुम becomes आप, commands become -इए and -लीजिए, and her hands clasp at her waist.
Gives the hour in whole hours by her father's watch, which runs two minutes fast ('nau baje'). Minutes only in an emergency ('Nau bajkar das.'), which is how the family knows it is one.
On the roof, with the chillies, the list stops: slow whole sentences with their verbs ('Mirchi bach gayi.'). It is the only time she speaks slowly.
Counts heads with one raised left forefinger, exactly as Nani does, in silence: the count is never said aloud (a head-count in speech is Nani's one album line).
catchphrases: 'Haan ji, boliye.' | 'हाँ जी, बोलिए।' | 'Yes, tell me.' (every phone call, every customer, and you)
'Nau baje. Shutter up.' | 'नौ बजे। शटर ऊपर।' | 'Nine o'clock. Shutter up.' (her one catchphrase with a number: the shutter hour, which her target allows)
'Aur kuch?' | 'और कुछ?' | 'Anything else?' (the counter's closer, which the family quotes back at her; it takes the place of 'Iska bill nahin.', now a rare line)
voice.exclamation: 'Had hai!' | 'हद है!' | English mode 'This is too much!', which is how Indian English says it. For exasperation only: the water at the door, the lights failing in an electrician's own house, a delivery gone wrong. Secular: it means 'this is the limit', it calls on no one, and it is never followed by any name. No one else in the cast uses it as an exclamation. She has no exclamation for joy: good news comes out as orders ('Tinku, mithai lao.').
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY, plain first: 'Meri galti.' | 'मेरी ग़लती।' | 'My mistake.', with the name ('Meri galti, Tinku.'). When her mistake cost someone, she names what she did and owns it in plain words, to an elder as to anyone: 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid meri galti thi.' | 'मास्टरजी, कल रात की ज़िद मेरी ग़लती थी।' | 'Masterji, I was stubborn last night. My mistake.'. No idiom: 'mere khaate mein daal do' is the sulky 'go on, blame me then', and khaata is her credit book. THANKS, GIVEN: plain words first, then a deed. To elders, 'Didi, aapne bahut kiya.' | 'दीदी, आपने बहुत किया।' | 'Didi, you did so much.', with something off the shelf put into their hands. To the young, 'Bahut achha kiya.' | 'बहुत अच्छा किया।' | 'That was really good.', and then something done for them ('Aaj raat ka khana mera.' | 'Dinner tonight is on me.'). When family reaches for a wallet at her counter: 'Aapse paise? Rehne dijiye.' | 'आपसे पैसे? रहने दीजिए।' | 'Money, from you? Put it away.'. 'Iska bill nahin.' survives only as a rare line, once a chapter at most, when a gift goes over the counter. THANKS, RECEIVED: the brush-off every elder in the north uses, 'Arre, isme kya.' | 'अरे, इसमें क्या।' | 'Oh, it's nothing.', and she turns straight to an order for someone else ('Tinku, agle ka bill banao.'). LOVE: mostly a deed: the red 'paid' pen laid down for you in January and the spare shop key in the album, each turned towards you, her hand coming back to her side; a handful of roof chillies for Nani every Sunday. When love comes out in speech it is a packed list that keeps its verb ('Torch, charger, extension, sab bag mein hai.') and the line every mother says on a platform ('Pahunchkar phone karna.').

'chinta mat karo' | 'don't worry' (she distrusts the line, which is Mama ji's); 'help' or 'madad' about herself; 'thak gayi' | 'I'm tired'; a vague time ('lagbhag', 'thodi der mein', 'around ten'): these are her character, not a word list

(Mausa ji's); 'Bas.' as the closer of an argument (Nani's); 'Suno, suno, suno!' and 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!' (Mausi's); 'Pakka?' at the end of a worry stack (Mama ji's); 'Correct?' and 'Tick.' (Mami's); 'Darj hai.' (Papa's); 'Next ball.' and 'Dead ball.' (Captain sahab's); 'Pehle ___.' as a tic (yours); 'Chai piyo.' as a sorry (Nani's); 'Hmm. Ho jayega.' (Mausa ji's). The common words inside these phrases are free.

'Mubarak ho' (cast-wide 4: unused for now; it and her 'Badhai ho!' are both everyday congratulations and take one ruling from the owner, and an Urdu-speaking reader checks that both sides are treated alike, India verdict 3)

a thumbs-up or any emoji (Mausa ji's and yours)

(now 'Ek paisa bhi kam nahin.'), and 'Iska bill nahin.' as a standing thank-you
address: To you: तुम in commands (देखो, लो, भेजो, लॉक करो, लेट जाओ), in 'who should' asks (किसे रखें?, कौन करे?, never कौन करेगा?) and in lines where you are not the doer (बाक़ी फ़ोन, सब तुम्हारे।); one line waits on the owner: 'Bahut achha kiya.', a past with ने where you are the doer and किया agrees with the thing done, cleared only if rule 66 gains that fourth shape or the native reader puts it on the build's cleared list; आप and -इए only when she is cross (आप ही गिन लीजिए।). No address word for you at all: never beta or a pet name, never बेटा, भैया or दीदी. On the phone her shop greeting reaches you too, and बोलिए marks no gender; once she knows the voice she drops to तुम with 'Achha, tum.', so the switch is heard.
To Nani: 'Amma' | 'अम्मा', with आप ('Amma, aap baithiye.'), the word all three of Nani's children use.
To Papa: no address word; she starts with the item ('Bhindi itni mehngi?'), or with a plain 'Suno,' on the phone, with तुम, equal respect. Of him, to you and Tinku: 'tumhare Papa'.
To Mama ji: 'Chhote' | 'छोटे', with तुम; 'Chhote ji' and आप when cross (and when he arrives late).
To Mausa ji: 'Jija ji' | 'जीजा जी', with आप.
To Tinku: 'Tinku', with तुम; 'Tinku ji' and आप when cross, in speech and in typing.
To Mami: 'Bhabhi' | 'भाभी', with तुम; 'tumhari Mami' when she speaks of her to you.
To Masterji and Captain sahab: their titles, with आप; both call her 'Bhabhi ji'.
To customers, wholesalers and hired hands: 'ji' and आप, always, with no comma before the ji ('Le jaiye ji.', 'Zaroor ji.'), and no kin word, so 'Bhaiya ji' stays Mami's.
samples: ORDER (to you and Tinku, Saturday, before the shutter): 'Tum bill, Tinku stock, main shutter.' | 'तुम बिल, टिंकू स्टॉक, मैं शटर।' | 'You on bills, Tinku on stock, me on the shutter.' (her shape for orders: people and jobs in one comma list with no verb)

THE GOAL OF THE MOMENT (chapter 3 opening, rules 37 and 43): 'Kichad saaf, maal upar, Shanivaar nau baje shutter.' | 'कीचड़ साफ़, माल ऊपर, शनिवार नौ बजे शटर।' | 'Mud out, stock up, shutter at nine on Saturday.' (the shutter hour, one of her two marked figures, as the chapter's target; never the number the two tie on)

TO MASTERJI (3.02, when he asks from his doorway whether all this mud can be gone by Saturday): 'Shutter apne waqt pe uthega, Masterji. Nau baje.' | 'शटर अपने वक़्त पर उठेगा, मास्टरजी। नौ बजे।' | 'The shutter goes up on time, Masterji. Nine o'clock.' (वक़्त as an everyday town word in her mouth, cast-wide 8)

A WHO-SHOULD ASK (chapter 3, to you): 'Haath chahiye, kichad aur maal ke liye. / Kise rakhein?' | 'हाथ चाहिए, कीचड़ और माल के लिए। / किसे रखें?' | 'We need hands, for the mud and the stock. / Who do we take on?' (रखें is a subjunctive and चाहिए never changes form, so neither marks a gender)

TO A CUSTOMER (the counter, any day): 'Haan ji, boliye. Fuse, switch ya wire?' | 'हाँ जी, बोलिए। फ़्यूज़, स्विच या वायर?' | 'Yes, tell me. Fuse, switch or wire?' (the shop greeting, then the list as a question)

TO A CUSTOMER who wants a part she is out of: 'Zaroor ji, kal tak mangwa deti hoon. / Naam likhwa dijiye.' | 'ज़रूर जी, कल तक मँगवा देती हूँ। / नाम लिखवा दीजिए।' | 'Of course, ji, I'll have it by tomorrow. / Just leave your name.' (ज़रूर as a town word; देती हूँ is her own voice, said to a customer)

TO THE WHOLESALER'S MAN who asks for the owner, the malik: 'Main hi hoon. Boliye, delivery kab?' | 'मैं ही हूँ। बोलिए, डिलीवरी कब?' | 'That's me. Tell me, when's the delivery?' (one beat at most, no general statement; straight to business)

WORRY (the flood, to Masterji over the wall): 'Masterji, fan, wire, switch, sab paani mein. Poora maal.' | 'मास्टरजी, फ़ैन, वायर, स्विच, सब पानी में। पूरा माल।' | 'Masterji, fans, wire, switches, all under water. The whole stock.' (the worry is the goods, not a sum)

WORRY, AN EMERGENCY (any night, to you): 'Nau bajkar das. Amma ka phone nahin aaya.' | 'नौ बजकर दस। अम्मा का फ़ोन नहीं आया।' | 'Ten past nine. Amma hasn't rung.' (emergency minutes, her second marked figure: Nani rings at nine, so silence is the alarm; check 3 flags आया, which agrees with फ़ोन, so a native reader clears it)

THE DODGE (asked by you how she is): 'Copper phir mehenga. Aur kuch?' | 'कॉपर फिर महँगा। और कुछ?' | 'Copper's up again. Anything else?' (a feeling changed into shop news with no figure, closed like a sale; महँगा agrees with कॉपर)

PRAISE (to you, after you count the drawer at closing): 'Ek paisa bhi kam nahin. / Galla lock karo, shutter neeche.' | 'एक पैसा भी कम नहीं। / गल्ला लॉक करो, शटर नीचे।' | 'Not a paisa short. / Lock the drawer, shutter down.' (her highest praise in the everyday idiom, then the next job)

THANKS, PLAIN (to Mausi after the flood basket, putting a new emergency light from the shelf into her hands): 'Didi, aapne bahut kiya. Ye light rakhiye.' | 'दीदी, आपने बहुत किया। ये लाइट रखिए।' | 'Didi, you did so much. Keep this light.' (plain words first, the gift after them)

THANKS, TO YOU (the evening you took every call in the shop): 'Bahut achha kiya. / Aaj raat ka khana mera.' | 'बहुत अच्छा किया। / आज रात का खाना मेरा।' | 'That was really good. / Dinner tonight is on me.' (plain thanks, then a deed: on a weekday, when Papa cooks. Rule 66 owner question: you are the doer here, and किया is a past with ने that agrees with the thing done, so it marks no gender, but rule 66 names only three shapes for तुम. The owner either adds this as a fourth shape or has the native reader clear the line onto the build's cleared list; no wording change if the owner agrees)

WHEN FAMILY TRIES TO PAY (Mausa ji, reaching for his wallet at her counter): 'Jija ji, aapse paise? Rehne dijiye.' | 'जीजा जी, आपसे पैसे? रहने दीजिए।' | 'Jija ji, money from you? Put it away.' (the gift with no code)

SORRY (to Masterji, the morning after she sent him back on the first flood night): 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid meri galti thi.' | 'मास्टरजी, कल रात की ज़िद मेरी ग़लती थी।' | 'Masterji, I was stubborn last night. My mistake.' (plain words, owned out loud to an elder; थी agrees with ज़िद and ग़लती, and the line is said to Masterji, not to you)

SORRY, PLAIN (to Tinku, whose carton count was right after all): 'Meri galti, Tinku. Tumhari ginti sahi thi.' | 'मेरी ग़लती, टिंकू। तुम्हारी गिनती सही थी।' | 'My mistake, Tinku. Your count was right.'

SAYING NO (to Mama ji, who has sent money again): 'Chhote, paise apne paas rakho. / Khud aao, Amma ke paas.' | 'छोटे, पैसे अपने पास रखो। / ख़ुद आओ, अम्मा के पास।' | 'Chhote, keep your money. / Come yourself, and see Amma.' (a no as a list of jobs)

GIVING CREDIT (the flood week, to a stranger from the lane who needs a fuse): 'Le jaiye ji. Khaate mein likh diya, aaram se.' | 'ले जाइए जी। खाते में लिख दिया, आराम से।' | 'Take it. It's in the book. Pay when you can.' (her turn in chapter 3: owing the lane is how a lane works; both scripts say khaata, as a small-town shop does, with no comma before ji)

THE OLD SHOP SAYING (chapter 3 only, before the flood, to a stranger who asks for credit; flat, never for a laugh): 'Udhaar? Kal.' | 'उधार? कल।' | 'Today cash, tomorrow credit.' (clipped from the shop sign आज नक़द, कल उधार; English mode uses the sign's own English, which Indian shops paint too; it stays in the chapter that later opens her credit book to the whole lane)

CROSS (to Tinku, five past nine on a Saturday): 'Tinku ji, nau baj gaye. Aap kahaan hain?' | 'टिंकू जी, नौ बज गए। आप कहाँ हैं?' | 'Tinku ji, it's nine. Where are you, may I ask?' (politeness rises: ji on a name that never carries it, आप; the shutter hour)

CROSS (to Mama ji, who offers to send city workmen): 'Chhote ji, aap hi chala lijiye. Chaabi ye rahi.' | 'छोटे जी, आप ही चला लीजिए। चाबी ये रही।' | 'Chhote ji, you run it, then. Here's the key.' (anger as politeness; the keys held out, then her fist closes on them)

EXCLAIMING (the water at the door, the first flood night): 'Had hai! / Paani darwaze tak. Balti, kapda, mains off karo.' | 'हद है! / पानी दरवाज़े तक। बाल्टी, कपड़ा, मेन्स ऑफ़ करो।' | 'This is too much! / Water's at the door. Buckets, cloths, mains off.' (her one exclamation, then the list)

COMFORT (to you, the first flood night, at two): 'Paani kal, maal parson, shutter Shanivaar. / Ab let jao. Baaki subah.' | 'पानी कल, माल परसों, शटर शनिवार। / अब लेट जाओ। बाक़ी सुबह।' | 'Water out tomorrow, stock the day after, shutter Saturday. / Lie down now. The rest can wait till morning.' (the schedule, then one plain care line; a command, so no gender, and not Mausa ji's So jao)

habits: Device: a plain black Android phone in a plain black case, the screen painted blank with every word laid on as live text (rule 30). It lives in the side pocket of her kameez and comes out wedged between her left ear and shoulder.

Script: Roman Hinglish (Hindi in Latin letters), all lowercase. Commas only: no full stops, no question marks, no exclamation marks, even when she asks ('khud kab aa rahe'). Her spelling drifts (chabi, chaabi); her trade nouns never do.

HER HABIT: she acknowledges with the shop's 'haan ji', typed alone as the whole reply, to her own children as to a customer. Never 'ok', never 'done', never a thumbs-up. Anyone in the house may type haan ji inside a message; a bare 'haan ji' as the whole answer, every time, is her.

Shape: the same comma list of people and jobs as her speech ('daal tum banao, shutter neeche, ghar aa rahi'), two to eight words, one message per thought, never a paragraph, never a greeting or a sign-off.
Thanks are typed in plain words with a deed or a care after them ('bahut achha kiya, ab ghar jao'), never in a code.

Figures: only when the fact itself is a figure and only in an emergency, so a digit from her is rare and means trouble (the flood night's '6 baje'). Prices stay on the photographed bills, painted blank.
When cross, her texts get polite too: 'ji' on the name and -इए on the verb ('tinku ji counter pe aaiye').
Photos: of bills and stock cartons, painted blank, each with the same caption, 'ye wala check karo' or 'ye wala'.
Voice notes when her hands are busy in the shop. They start with her shop greeting even though she is the one calling ('haan ji boliye, achha tum'), shown as live text.

Emoji: none, ever (the thumbs-up is Mausa ji's, and your own reply to her). No stickers, no good-morning pictures (those are Papa's). The one news she sends unasked is the power-cut times, retyped the moment she hears them, shown as a message card (no group chat appears in the game).

Speed: reads within a minute between nine in the morning and half past eight at night, and replies only when she has the answer. Nothing between the shutter coming down and the end of Nani's nine o'clock call, and never after nine, so a late message from her means trouble. The flood night is the one time all year.
She never texts Nani. Nani rings her at nine every night, and Mummy waits for it.
Types fast with her left thumb, phone in her left hand, because her right hand is holding the keys or the pen.

changed: COMMON FILLERS FREED (cast-wide 1). Her never list no longer bans arre, achha, chalo, suno, dekho, bas, theek hai, pakka, galti, galat, fikr, waqt or zaroor, and 'haan ji' is no longer hers alone. What other people keep are phrases and exclamations ('Arre waah.', a one-word 'Theek.', 'Bas.' as a closer, 'Suno, suno, suno!'), and only those stay off her. New lines use the freed words: 'Suno, aaj der hogi.' to Papa, 'Chalo, ab yaad rahega.', 'Arre Jija ji, isme kya.', 'Koi baat nahin.'. Her tell is the whole phone greeting 'Haan ji, boliye.', and in typing a bare 'haan ji' as the whole reply.

VERB + kar/ho SHARED (cast-wide 2). The claim that the English verb + kar/ho is hers alone is gone from mix, tics and uses. She is marked by where she aims it: the shop's English at home, as in any electrician's house ('MCB check karo', 'mains off karo').

SORRY AND THANKS IN PLAIN WORDS (cast-wide 3, real-India 1). Sorry is 'Meri galti.' first; the coined 'Ye mere hisaab mein.' becomes plain words, 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid meri galti thi.' (the khaata idiom tried in between is gone: see the final polish). Thanks given: 'Didi, aapne bahut kiya.' and 'Bahut achha kiya.', with the gift or a deed after the words; 'Aapse paise? Rehne dijiye.' when family tries to pay. Thanks received: the brush-off 'Arre, isme kya.'. 'Iska bill nahin.' leaves her catchphrases and is a rare line, once a chapter at most; 'Aur kuch?' takes its place as her third catchphrase. Her thanks to the young is a deed for them, not the next job, so it stays clear of Nani's 'Ab ye bhi.'.

CONGRATULATION (cast-wide 4, real-India 3). Moment 3 now says 'Badhai ho!', in English 'Many congratulations!', so it does not copy Mami's flat 'Congratulations.'. Owner question: if 'Badhai ho' is not allowed under rule 3, the line drops it and reads 'Achha, tum! Naukri? / Letter bhejo, counter pe lagaungi.'. 'Mubarak ho' is on her never list, as the note asks.

THE REGISTER SWITCH ON THE CALL (Hindi-rules 2). Moment 3 adds the recognition beat 'Achha, tum!' between the shop greeting (बोलिए) and the तुम command (भेजो), so the drop from आप to तुम is heard, as in her voice note; the address table and her first tic now say so.

THE CREDIT BOOK IN HINDI (Hindi-rules 1). Hindi mode says खाता, not क्रेडिट बुक, and drops the comma inside 'ले जाइए जी'; Hinglish now says khaata too (final polish). Customers get 'ji' with no comma before it.

WARMTH IN COMFORT (real-India 2, cast-wide 9). The 2 am schedule gets a second bubble of plain care, 'Ab let jao. Baaki subah.'. A new morning-after comfort keeps her list but gives it its verb: 'Shutter hai, counter hai, haath hain. / Kaafi hai.'. The platform goodbye keeps its packed list, adds 'hai' and the line every mother says ('Pahunchkar phone karna.'), and moment 11 opens with 'Koi baat nahin.' before the jobs.

FEWER CLIPPED LINES (cast-wide 9). The register now gives her two shapes: comma lists with no verb for orders, plans and a no; short whole sentences with hai or hoon for comfort and love ('sab bag mein hai', 'Main glass laati hoon.'). Test lines 2, 3, 5, 6, 10 and 11 now carry their verbs.

TRADER STEREOTYPE (real-India 4). The calendar joke ('Calendar muft. Keel ka bill alag.') is cut; 1.02 is wordless or 'Dukaan se.'. 'Udhaar? Kal.' stays only in chapter 3, before the flood, the chapter that later opens her credit book to the whole lane, and is now named as the clipped shop sign आज नक़द, कल उधार.

ENGLISH MODE (real-India 5, cast-wide 10). 'That's the limit!' becomes 'This is too much!'; 'Yes, go ahead.' becomes 'Yes, tell me.', the way Indian English answers a phone; moment 11 becomes 'Tinku, cloth. I'll get a glass. You, a biscuit.'; 'Put that on my account' is gone with the khaata sorry (final polish); 'Okra, that dear?' becomes 'Bhindi, this expensive?'; 'You're looking at her' becomes 'That's me.'; 'Credit? Tomorrow.' becomes the sign's own 'Today cash, tomorrow credit.'.

REAL IDIOMS ONLY. 'Ek rupaya kam nahin.' becomes the everyday 'Ek paisa bhi kam nahin.'; the coined sorry becomes plain words ('meri galti thi'); 'Copper phir chadh gaya.' uses the trader's own verb for a price going up.

SHARED BITS (cast-wide 6). Moment 2 moves off food, where five people reached for the cold dinner, to Amma: 'Amma aapka raasta dekhte-dekhte so gayin.', still with her cross politeness ('Aaiye, Chhote ji.').

TOWN WORDS (cast-wide 8). ज़रूर and वक़्त are in her mouth as everyday words ('Zaroor ji, kal tak mangwa deti hoon.', 'Shutter apne waqt pe uthega, Masterji.'), and ज़रूरत is in her uses, so these words belong to the town and not to the tailor.
RULE 22 GUARD (cast-wide 5). A new never line: near any report beat, none of her paper words may sound like a demand for proof ('bill dikhao', 'likh ke do', 'receipt', 'saboot').

KEPT, AS THE READERS MARKED TRUE: 'Haan ji, boliye.' even to her own children; 'Had hai!'; 'Main hi hoon. Boliye, delivery kab?'; 'Bhindi itni mehngi? Kal se sabzi main laaungi.'; 'Tinku ji, nau baj gaye. Aap kahaan hain?'; 'Chhote ji, aap hi chala lijiye. Chaabi ye rahi.'; the credit book opened in the flood week; 'Band? Unka shutter aaj bhi utha.'. Also unchanged: her essence (she runs the family like the shop), want (the shutter at nine, owing no one), fear (the shutter staying down, owing anyone), contradiction (swore never to sit behind a counter like her mother, runs hers exactly like her), the cost of her pride on the first flood night, the shutter hour and emergency minutes as her only figures, the dodge, 'Aur kuch?', the shop's English at home, her rising politeness when cross, the roof chillies, the address table and her typing habits.

FOR THE READERS (rule 65). A Hindi-first reader checks that 'Pahunchkar phone karna' and 'Kaafi hai' read as free of gender, and clears every rule 66 flag noted on the lines (आया, महँगा, गया, ग़लती, रहेगा, थी, करना, किया, काफ़ी, तुम्हारे, गई, भरा था, भी, जी: each agrees with a thing, is an infinitive or a word that never changes form, or is a particle, and none agrees with the player). The owner answers whether 'Badhai ho' passes rule 3, and whether rule 66 gains a fourth shape for 'Bahut achha kiya.' (final polish, rule 66).

FINAL POLISH, MOMENT 5 (Hindi rules and real-India 1). 'Chalo, ye mere khaate mein daal do.' used the तुम command to a family with Nani and other elders in it, and the khaata blame idiom read as the sulky 'go on, blame me then' straight after 'Meri galti.'. The Hindi note's fix, 'Chalo, ye mere khaate mein.', drops the verb but keeps the idiom the real-India note retires, so the line keeps the Hindi note's principle (no command, so no politeness level) in plain words: 'Achha? Meri galti. / Chalo, ab yaad rahega.' | 'अच्छा? मेरी ग़लती। / चलो, अब याद रहेगा।' | 'Oh? My mistake. / Right, I'll remember that.'. If the owner prefers the Hindi note's exact wording, it drops in with no other change.

FINAL POLISH, THE SORRY TO MASTERJI (real-India 1). 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid, mere khaate mein daaliye.' read as a coined apology; it is now the plain 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid meri galti thi.' | 'मास्टरजी, कल रात की ज़िद मेरी ग़लती थी।' | 'Masterji, I was stubborn last night. My mistake.'. The khaata idiom leaves her sorry and goes on her never list; khaata is only her real credit book.

FINAL POLISH, KHAATA IN HINGLISH (real-India 2). 'Credit book mein likh diya' sounded translated; Hinglish now says 'Khaate mein likh diya', as the Hindi already did, and her mix and uses name the book khaata in both scripts.

FINAL POLISH, THE TEA CUP CUT (real-India 3). 'Tinku, ye cup return karo.' was a writer's joke for the one person who never jokes. Moment 4 is now 'Tinku, cheeni kam, dobara banao.' | 'टिंकू, चीनी कम, दोबारा बनाओ।' | 'Tinku, less sugar, make it again.', her list shape with no gimmick. The counter-English tic now rests on what is natural in an electrician's house ('MCB check karo', 'mains off karo'), and 'return karo' leaves her uses.

FINAL POLISH, RULE 66 OWNER QUESTION (cast). 'Bahut achha kiya.' to you is a past with ने where you are the doer; किया agrees with the thing done and marks no gender, but rule 66 names only commands, 'who should' asks and lines where you are not the doer. No wording change: the owner either adds 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' to rule 66 as a fourth shape, or has the native reader clear the line onto the build's cleared list. The sample and her address table now say so.
